GDI

Disinformation

Concept note prepared for USAID - August 2022
Background
GDI, a global non-profit organization, assesses open web domains for their risk of carrying
disinformation. We use an expert-validated methodology which combines Al and human review
to evaluate a site's:
• Content: a human review assesses for clickbait, bias, hate speech, sensationalism and
so on; and
• Operations: policies and safeguards relating to, for example, transparency of
ownership, editorial independence, conflicts of interest, errors and corrections.
We consider disinformation in the context of "adversarial narratives" (as opposed to a
"true/false" binary); "adversarial narratives" are used by disinformation actors to inflame social
tensions, and to exploit and amplify the perceived grievances of individuals, groups and
institutions. In this way, disinformation actors seek to delegitimize governments, principles,
practices, and policies.
We have reviewed the media markets of 19 countries to date, including those where
democracy is more fragile and/or political extremism more prevalent (Brazil, Nigeria, Germany,
Malaysia), and are currently working on Ukraine, Indonesia, Vietnam and Turkey.
Thanks to the support of its funders, GDI was able to take a critical early step in developing
tools for the advertising technology ('ad tech') companies which place ads online on behalf of
their clients. For example, the 'GDI Dynamic Exclusion List' (of the 2500+ worst offending
disinformation sites) is currently embedded in the systems of thirteen global ad tech
companies, including IAS, Peer39 and Oracle (three of the key players). Subscribers to this
GDI tool are able to block these domains from their online bidding systems and divert clients'
ad spend away from disinforming content.
GDI is dedicated to reducing the impact of disinformation on democracies, and on the systems
of civil society which uphold human rights (including an independent and transparent media).
We are committed to neutrality, remaining steadfastly bipartisan by working with (and seeking
and receiving funding from) organizations across the political spectrum.

Proposed Activities
GDI proposes to carry out Media Market Reviews (MMRs) in three of USAID's priority countries
in order to identify online news and information sources that are at high-risk of disinforming
readers. We develop a sample of pertinent online news sources for each market, training a local
research team to execute GDI's data collection methodology and calculate risk rating scores
based on the data collected. We support the local team in drafting a report on disinformation
risks in the media market. Each project takes roughly six months to complete and yields two key
outputs:
1. Risk ratings per site that can beshared privately with USAID (as well as with licensees
of GDI's data); and
2. A public report which supports local stakeholders (journalists, civil society, etc.) in
addressing disinformation risk factors in their own media environment.
We propose to conduct MMRs in Moldova, Zambia, and Armenia. Disinformation undermines
development goals in different ways in each context. The Fourth Estate is critical to
development and democracy, but underdevelopment is a risk factor for disinformation, tempting
government intervention in the media space. GDI believes that third-party support for a media
environment free of disinformation and its harms is a critical component of modern democratic
development.
Moldova
GDI proposes to work with USAID to identify a partner organization that can execute GDI's
MMR methodology for the Moldovan media market.
Moldova is experiencing an ongoing information war' in the wake of Russia's invasion of
Ukraine. Internet actors are turning the influx of Ukrainian refugees into a divisive issue in
Moldovan society, which has enormous implications for peace and security, development, and
democratic stability. Furthermore, pro-Russian narratives are thought to be an attempt to turn
the country away from the West and toward Russia. In this context, support for trustworthy,
quality journalism can act as a bulwark against other influences.
Zambia
Zambia is a strategic choice for this proposal because the context very much calls for such a
study, and GDI has an existing partnership in place to undertake the work.

Reporters Without Borders has identified a number of vulnerabilities in Zambia's media
environment, but also reports that, for the first time in many years, no journalists were detained
by the state at the end of 2021,2 following the August 2021 election of Hakainde Hichilema.
President Hichilema ran on a promise to end government interference in Zambian media.
However, even amidst a respite from political interference, independent journalism faces
economic challenges, making this a crucial moment to direct advertising spending toward
quality media outlets.
Based on our successful collaboration in Nigeria, GDI is currently developing a strategic
regional partnership with Paradigm Initiative, a digital rights organization with offices in six
sub-Saharan African countries, including Zambia.3 Paradigm Initiative will coordinate a team of
Zambian researchers to undertake the review in English and the local language(s) relevant to
the media market.
Armenia
In Its latest annual report "Nations in Transit 2022"
", the Freedom House organization has drawn
attention to regression in the field of media independence in Armenia and to the new article in
the Armenian criminal code on "grave insult".
Further,
at the time of writing, reports of escalation in Nagorno-Karabakh/Artsakh claim that
Azerbaijan has been violating the ceasefire regime and trying to capture new positions in the
Northern and North-western parts of Nagorno-Karabakh. Disinformation about this escalation
will likely spread very quickly in Russia, with those narratives further escalating the conflicts
themselves.

USAID / Platform Intervention Pilot
USAID has indicated that its growing relationships with the large online platforms, including
Alphabet and Meta, offer an opportunity to take action in these three countries based on the
data that GDI's MMRs produce. To take advantage of this unique opportunity for impact, GDI
proposes to work cooperatively with USAID to identify the highest risk media in each country
and guide work with the platforms to take action in the following areas:

• Defund: Work with platforms to defund high disinformation risk media in these
countries, including through advertising and other audience monetisation techniques.
• Downrank: Work with platforms to downrank this content in search, newsfeed, and
other recommender systems that suggest content to users in these countries.
• Deplatform: Work with platforms to block or eliminate the most egregious
disinformation peddlers in these countries that violate existing platform policies, as
identified by the GDI MMRs.
